h1: Does a small business actually need an SEO agency?
metaTitle: Do Small Businesses Need an SEO Agency?
metaDescription: Most small businesses don't need an SEO agency yet. Five checks, the margin maths behind a retainer, and a 90-day plan you can genuinely run yourself.
answer: Most small businesses don't need an SEO agency yet. A retainer only pays back when one customer is worth roughly ₹10,000 in gross margin or more, and when people already search for what you sell. Below that, a complete Google Business Profile and twenty real reviews beat any ₹40,000 retainer.
takeaways: Run the **margin maths first**. At ₹40,000/mo, a business earning ₹500 gross per customer needs 80 extra customers a month just to break even on the fee.
For a single-location business, most of the winnable upside sits in **Google Business Profile and reviews** — both free, both doable in a weekend plus a habit.
SEO surfaces demand that already exists. If nobody searches your category in your city, no agency changes that.
The honest sequence is: fix the profile, fix the site, fix the phone, *then* consider a retainer.

sections.h2: Five checks before you hire anyone
body: We turn down more small businesses than we sign, and it's almost always for one of these five reasons. Run them yourself before you take a single sales call. They take an afternoon and they'll save you a year of retainer fees.
numbered: **Does search demand exist?** Open Google Keyword Planner, or just search your category plus your city and look at what comes back. If the results are national aggregators and nothing local, or if there's genuinely nothing, people aren't finding your category this way. SEO surfaces existing demand. It doesn't invent it.
**Is one customer worth ₹10,000 or more in gross margin?** Or worth ₹3,000 repeated twelve times? If neither, the arithmetic in the next section is going to hurt.
**Can you handle more enquiries?** A dentist with one chair and a full book has a capacity problem, not a marketing problem. More leads makes it worse.

**Does your site convert the traffic you already have?** Check Search Console for the last 90 days. If you're getting 400 clicks a month and closing nobody, adding 400 more changes nothing. Fix the page, the price clarity and the phone number before you buy reach.

**Can you fund twelve months?** SEO compounds. Three months of retainer followed by a cancellation is money set on fire — you pay for the setup and quit before the return arrives. If twelve months at your quoted rate isn't comfortable, don't start.

callout.title: About that ₹5,000-a-month package
callout.body: At that price nobody is doing SEO. They're running an automated audit, spinning four blog posts and firing your URL at a directory list. It doesn't just fail — a junk link profile takes real work to undo later. Free and careful beats cheap and careless.

sections.h2: The margin maths that actually decides it
body: Here's the calculation almost nobody runs before signing. Take the monthly fee, divide by your gross margin per customer, and you get the number of extra customers you need every month just to break even on the fee — before you've made a rupee of profit on it.
We're using ₹40,000/month, which is the low end of a serious retainer in India and where our own smaller-site SEO starts. Three rules before you run it on your own numbers:
bullets: Use **gross margin**, not revenue. A ₹50,000 order carrying ₹4,000 of margin is a ₹4,000 customer.
Add lifetime value if it's genuinely repeat business. A gym member at ₹1,500/month for eighteen months is a ₹27,000 customer, not a ₹1,500 one.
Then roughly double the break-even figure. You want the channel to pay for itself *and* return something, and a meaningful share of what SEO brings in won't close.

sections.h2: When your Google Business Profile is the whole job
body: If you serve customers from one address or one service area — a clinic, a studio, a workshop, a restaurant, a local practice — most of your winnable search traffic lives in the map pack, not the blue links. And the map pack responds to things you control directly, for free.

The local ranking inputs Google is open about are relevance, distance and prominence. You can't move distance. You can move the other two in an afternoon, and no agency does it better than an owner who actually knows the business.

Here's the uncomfortable bit for our industry: for a single-location business with a decent website, a fully-built [Google Business Profile](/glossary/google-business-profile) plus a steady review habit will out-perform the first six months of most ₹25,000 retainers. We'd rather you knew that from us.
bullets: Primary category set precisely — "orthodontist", not "dentist", if that's what you actually are. This one field moves more than most on-page work.
Every service and product listed, each with its own description. Most profiles leave this empty.
Real photos, added monthly. Interior, exterior, team, work in progress.
Hours correct, including holidays. A wrong "closed" costs you that click permanently.
Q&A seeded with the questions you answer on the phone twenty times a week.
Reviews: ask every satisfied customer, in person, with a short link. Reply to all of them, including the bad ones, without sounding like a legal department.

sections.h2: A 90-day plan you can run yourself
body: This is what we'd tell a single-location business to do instead of hiring us. Roughly four hours a week, no tools beyond Search Console, which is free.

callout.title: Freeze the number before week one
callout.body: Write down your enquiries from search over the last 90 days, from your own records. At day 90 you compare against it. Without that frozen number you'll have opinions instead of evidence — which is exactly how agencies get paid for nothing.

bullets: Claim and verify your Google Business Profile. Fill every field, including the ones that feel pointless.
Set up Google Search Console and connect it to your site. This becomes your evidence file for everything that follows.
Write down the baseline. Enquiries per month from search, right now.
Generate your review short link and put it on the invoice, the WhatsApp follow-up, and a card at the counter.
Ask in person at the moment of relief — after the treatment, after the delivery, after the fix. Not by email three days later.
Reply to every review inside 48 hours, and name the service in the reply.

subs.h3: Weeks 5–8 — make the site do its job
bullets: One page per service you actually sell, each answering: what it is, who it's for, what decides the cost, and what happens next.
Phone number as a tap-to-call link on mobile, above the fold. WhatsApp too, if that's how your customers behave — and in India it usually is.
Name, address and phone identical everywhere they appear. Same format, same suite number, same spelling.
Compress your images. Most small business sites in India are slow because of one 4MB hero photo.

subs.h3: Weeks 9–12 — write the three pages people search for
bullets: The price page. Even a range with the factors that move it. "Contact for pricing" loses to anyone who publishes a number.
The comparison page — the choice your customer is genuinely agonising over between two options.
The area page, but only if you truly serve multiple areas and can say something specific about each. Two honest pages beat fifteen templated ones.
Then open Search Console: are you appearing for more distinct queries than in week one? That's the signal, and it moves before revenue does.

sections.h2: Four cheaper things that work first
body: Before a retainer, spend the money here. Each of these is a one-off or a fraction of the monthly cost, and each one removes a reason SEO would have failed anyway.
bullets: **A one-off technical audit and fix.** A few days of a good freelancer's time, once, beats twelve months of a bad agency. See [what an SEO audit is](/answers/what-is-an-seo-audit).

**One month of paid search.** ₹20,000 on Google Ads tells you in three weeks what SEO takes six months to reveal: whether people search, whether they click, and whether they buy. If the ads don't convert, SEO on the same keywords wouldn't have either. Our [performance marketing](/performance) work starts at ₹40,000/mo, but a solo test costs less.
**Better photos and a booking flow that works.** Unglamorous, and it lifts every channel you already have.

**A freelancer on a small monthly.** Below roughly ₹40,000/month a good freelancer usually beats a cheap agency — fewer overheads, and you get the specialist rather than a junior. The trade-off is range. See [agency vs freelancer](/compare/agency-vs-freelancer).

sections.h2: The point where hiring stops being premature
body: There's a fairly clean line. Hire an agency when the free work has already produced something and you've run out of the ability to keep going — not when you're hoping someone else will start the fire for you.
In practice, four conditions have to be true at once:
numbered: Your gross margin per customer clears roughly ₹10,000, or your repeat value does.
Search Console already shows you appearing for queries you didn't pay for — proof the demand is real.
You have the capacity to serve more customers this quarter.
You can commit twelve months of budget without it hurting.

callout.title: What we'd charge, and what we'd guarantee
callout.body: Our SEO starts at ₹75,000/mo, with smaller sites from ₹40,000, ex-GST. The guarantee is deliberately narrow: we freeze your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic search on day one, and if we haven't beaten that number in 90 days we keep working free until we do. We never promise a specific position for a specific keyword — nobody controls Google's index. Numbers on [our pricing page](/pricing). And if you're not ready, we'll say so; a client who churns in month four is worse for us than one we never signed.

faqs.q: Is SEO worth it for a small business in India?
faqs.a: It's worth it when one customer is worth roughly ₹10,000 or more in gross margin, when demand already exists for what you sell, and when you can fund twelve months. For a low-margin, single-location business, a complete Google Business Profile and a review habit deliver more per rupee than any retainer.

faqs.q: Can a small business do its own SEO?
faqs.a: For a single-location business, genuinely yes. Claim and complete your Google Business Profile, build a review habit, give each service its own page, publish your prices, and fix your site speed. That covers most of the winnable upside. Competitive national keyword sets are where an agency's range starts to earn its fee.

faqs.q: What's the minimum sensible SEO budget for a small business?
faqs.a: In India, roughly ₹40,000/month for an agency doing real work on a small site. Below ₹25,000 you're funding a freelancer's part-time attention, which can still be fine — as long as you know that's what you're buying and don't expect four disciplines from one person.

faqs.q: How long before a small business sees results from SEO?
faqs.a: Local map pack work can move in four to eight weeks because the inputs are direct and under your control. Blue-link rankings on anything competitive take three to six months for real movement and six to twelve to compound. Anyone quoting faster is either buying links or describing a smaller problem than yours.

faqs.q: Should I hire an SEO agency or run Google Ads first?
faqs.a: Ads first, if you're unsure whether the demand converts. A month of paid search tells you in three weeks what SEO takes six months to reveal — whether people search, click and buy. If ads don't convert at a sane cost per lead, SEO on the same keywords wouldn't have either.

faqs.q: Do I need an SEO agency if I only serve one city?
faqs.a: Usually not at the start. Single-city businesses win in the map pack, and the map pack responds to your category, your reviews, your photos and your consistency — all free and all faster done by the owner. Hire when you've maxed that out and need site-wide content and links to grow further.
